writing.summary: Accept several string-like types when the operation only needs a borrowed view.
writing.rule: Ask for ownership only when the operation needs to keep or consume the value.
writing.explanation:
A function that only inspects text does not need a String allocation from every caller. A borrowed `&str` is often the simplest signature. `AsRef<str>` is useful when an API intentionally accepts several owned or borrowed string-like types and immediately obtains a string slice from them. It is a cheap reference conversion, not a general parsing or validation mechanism.

The example accepts a generic input, calls `as_ref()`, trims surrounding whitespace, and returns the number of Unicode scalar values. It never stores a reference after the call returns. Taking T by value still moves an owned String passed directly; callers that want to keep it can pass a reference. Generic syntax does not repeal ownership rules.

Choose the narrowest useful contract. A public function taking `&str` is easy to read and accepts `&String` through coercion. An `AsRef<Path>` parameter can be convenient for a file adapter, but path conversion does not grant filesystem permission. Similarly, `AsRef<str>` does not prove a string is a valid URL, port, or record. Keep the validated domain constructor from the earlier lesson as a separate operation.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab calls the same function with a string literal, a String, and a borrowed String. It includes accented text and an emoji so byte length cannot accidentally pass as character count. Rust chars are Unicode scalar values; they are not the same as user-perceived grapheme clusters, so describe the result precisely rather than calling it a universal display width.
writing.task: Trim surrounding whitespace and count Unicode scalar values for any AsRef<str> input. This is not byte length or grapheme count. In the Crabrix app, open the compiler lab and complete the supplied function in solution.rs. The reading question is a separate exercise.
writing.success: The local compiler accepts the changed solution and the separate verification harness finishes all normal and boundary cases. Printing a success message alone does not complete this lab.
writing.question: If an owned String is passed by value to fn f<T: AsRef<str>>(value: T), is the original still available?
answers: No, unless it was borrowed or cloned before the call
Only when the text is ASCII
writing.feedback: AsRef supplies a borrowed view inside the function. Passing the owned argument by value still moves it.

recall.question: What does this print, and why do the two numbers differ?
recall.answer: `2 8`: after trimming, `É` and the crab are two Unicode scalar values. `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes of the untrimmed string: two spaces, two bytes for `É`, and four for the crab. Passing `&owned` leaves the `String` usable.

recall.question: Why doesn't accepting `impl AsRef<str>` remove the need for a validating constructor such as `Port::from_str`?
recall.answer: `AsRef<str>` is only a cheap reference conversion that gives you a `&str` view; it says nothing about the text's contents. Whether the string is a valid port, URL or record still has to be checked by a separate, fallible operation.

depth.misconception: AsRef means arguments can never be moved.
depth.correction: The conversion is borrowed, but the parameter's ownership mode still matters.

traceSteps.title: Accept
traceSteps.detail: Choose a borrowed slice or a justified generic input.

traceSteps.title: View
traceSteps.detail: Call as_ref only for the lifetime of the operation.

traceSteps.title: Specify
traceSteps.detail: Count scalar values, not bytes or grapheme clusters.
